AM3S-01.note: Mode is unambiguous: 6 appears 3 times, 13 twice. The second repeated value (13) is the point of the item and is the one distractor doing real work; 10 (median) and 16 (max) are wrong-statistic pulls rather than errors in finding a mode, which is why this is plausible and not strong.

AM3S-02.note: 14 - 3 = 11, unambiguous given the plot renders the lone dot at 3. The item depends entirely on that dot being visible and clearly separated from the 5s; if the rendered plot crowds them, 9 becomes defensible. 9 (skip the low outlier) is the only distractor tied to a real reading error; 6 is the mode and 14 the max.

AM3S-03.note: Factors of 24 in 1-12: 1,2,3,4,6,8,12 -> 7/12. 6/12 (factors of 12 instead of 24) is a genuinely strong distractor and 5/12 (excluding 1 and the number itself out of habit) is real. 3/12 is the weak one - no student computes 'factors greater than 4'; its actual pull is as a generic small fraction. Denominators are uniformly 12, so nothing is given away by form.

AM3S-04.note: 8 primes in 1-20 -> 8/20 = 2/5. Every distractor is a named misconception: 7/20 drops 2, 9/20 admits 1, 1/2 counts all odds. Worth flagging that the key is the only option a student must reduce to recognise (they compute 8/20 and find no 8/20); 1/2 is also reduced so this is not a one-sided form tell, but it is the item most sensitive to a careless scan.

AM3S-05.note: Independent draws from two bags, (2/5)(4/5) = 8/25. 3/5 (pool all 10 marbles) and 2/5 (Bag A only) are the two standard failures; 17/25 is the complement. Unambiguous - the stem says one marble from each bag, so no replacement question arises.

AM3S-06.note: Inclusive OR on {2,4,6,7,8} = 5/8. 'Greater than 5' is strictly greater and cannot be read as 5-or-more without changing the answer, but the phrasing is standard and the boundary distractor 7/8 (double-counting 6 and 8) is the exact error the item is built to catch. 3/8 and 1/2 are the two single-event answers.

AM3S-07.note: 5x4x3 = 60. 'Exactly one of each' closes off any subset reading. 12 (add), 20 (stop after two factors), 27 ((5+4)x3) are all real add-vs-multiply failures. Standard early-section counting item.

AM3S-08.note: 16/100 = 4/25. 'Lies entirely inside' is the clause that makes this exclusive - without it the overlap would be undetermined. 2/5 (side ratio instead of area ratio) is the intended trap and is the most common real error; 21/25 is the complement. Note this is the second complement-bearing option set in a row (05, 08), see cross-item note on AM3S-24.

AM3S-09.note: 740 - 58 + 88 = 770, mean 77. The sum-then-adjust step is what makes this medium rather than easy. 71 (subtract the per-item correction instead of adding) and 74 (assume no effect) are real; 104 adds the full 30 to the mean, which is the named error but lands so far outside the plausible band that few students would keep it. Not weak, but the weakest of the three.

AM3S-10.note: 2(6)(4)/(10)(9) = 48/90 = 8/15. 'Without replacement' is stated, so 12/25 (the with-replacement answer) is a clean trap rather than an ambiguity. 7/15 is the match complement and 1/3 is both-red. Every distractor is the endpoint of a named path.

AM3S-11.note: (18-6) + (14-6) = 20 of 30 = 2/3. 'Exactly one' is explicit, which is what separates this from the at-least-one reading (26/30) - note that at-least-one is NOT among the options, so a student who misreads gets no confirmation and must reconsider; that is a design choice worth keeping. 2/5 (soccer-only), 1/5 (both), 2/15 (neither) are all real.

AM3S-12.note: (2/3)(1/2) + (1/3)(1) = 2/3. Coincidence worth noting: the answer 2/3 equals the probability of drawing a fair coin, so a student with the wrong model can arrive at the right number by luck - but no option rewards a cleaner wrong path, so exclusivity holds. 3/4 (unweighted average) and 5/6 (add the probabilities) are the two real failures.

AM3S-13.note: 21 of 48 = 43.75%. '3 or more' is unambiguous and the option set punishes all three misreadings: 25% (more than 3), 75% (3 or fewer), 56.25% (fewer than 3). Depends on the bar graph rendering exact readable heights - all six values are multiples of 3, which helps. Two complementary pairs sit in this set (25/75 and 43.75/56.25) and the key is in the non-round pair, which is mildly informative to a blind guesser.

AM3S-14.note: Missing cell 80 - 30 = 50; 50/200 = 1/4. The joint-vs-conditional distinction is the point, and 5/12 is exactly the conditional - a strong distractor. The margins are internally consistent (70+50=120, 50+30=80, 120+80=200), so the '?' is recoverable two ways and both give 50, which is what makes this exclusive.

AM3S-15.note: 15 of 36 outcomes. Every option shares denominator 36 so form gives nothing away, and all three distractors are boundary errors: 10/36 (strictly greater than 8), 26/36 (8 or less), 21/36 (7 or less). This is the cleanest boundary item in the batch.

AM3S-16.note: Graded EASY against the real section, not medium as commissioned - (first+last)/2 on an evenly spaced run is a recall fact, and even brute-forcing it is one step. Distractor quality is the weakest in the batch: 28 (range) and 29 (count) are answers to different questions rather than errors in computing a mean, so a student who knows what 'mean' means can eliminate both on sight and the item collapses to 26 vs 32. Not weak enough to fail - mean/range confusion is real - but this is the item to strengthen.

AM3S-17.note: 32/400 = 8%. 10% (unweighted average of 15% and 5%) is the canonical weighted-average trap and is the reason this item earns its place; 20% (add the rates) and 4.5% (one supplier's defects over the whole population) are both named. Group sizes 120 and 280 are deliberately unequal, which is what makes 10% wrong and detectable.

AM3S-18.note: Mean is 55/5 = 11, and removing a value equal to the mean is the only value that preserves it - unique, so exclusive. Distractors are the min, median and max, i.e. positional pulls rather than arithmetic endpoints; a student who computes the mean at all is done instantly, and one who does not is guessing among three shapes. Plausible, not strong. Also the only item in the batch where the options are simply the data values, so a blind solver sees nothing but the list.

AM3S-19.note: Q1 = 13, Q3 = 18.5, IQR = 5.5, fence = 26.75. Exclusive ONLY because the stem defines Q1 and Q3 as the medians of the halves - without that sentence, the 12-and-19 convention is defensible and 29.5 becomes a second correct answer. That definition is load-bearing and must not be trimmed. 29.5 (the other quartile convention), 34.25 (min-to-Q3 as the spread), 69.5 (range for IQR) are all named paths. Hard: long chain, non-round result, and 42 is a visible decoy outlier that plays no role in the computation.

AM3S-20.note: (3/5)(3/5)(2/5) = 18/125. Graded MEDIUM, not hard - once a student sees that the first two flips are forced, it is three multiplications, and the common denominator 125 signals the intended shape. 27/125 (no heads in three), 50/125 (the third flip alone, and deliberately left unreduced from 2/5 so it does not stand out), 98/125 (at least one head) are all real endpoints.

AM3S-21.note: 11 of 16 sequences. Graded MEDIUM, not hard - 'at least 2 of 4 fair flips' is a standard mid-section item reachable by 1 - P(0 or 1) with no combinatorial machinery. 5/16 is the complement computed but not subtracted, which is the single most common real failure here, and 15/16 answers the threshold-1 question. Note this is the third consecutive item whose distractor set contains its own complement (20, 21, 22).

AM3S-22.note: 7p - 3(1-p) = 10p - 3 = 0, p = 3/10. Exclusive on the standard reading that the $10 is what the player is handed and the $3 is already spent; 'pays $3 to play' and 'is handed $10' make net = $7, and no option corresponds to the alternative reading, so there is nothing to defend. Hard: expected value plus solving for a probability is at the top of the ACT's range, and the coincidence that the answer reduces to cost/prize will read as luck to most students. 3/13 and 7/13 (cost or net over cost+prize) are the real traps.

AM3S-23.note: C(9,3) - C(5,3) = 84 - 10 = 74. Every distractor is a named endpoint: 84 (ignore the constraint), 40 (exactly one teacher), 30 (exactly two). 40 + 30 + 4 = 74 is the direct route, so a student who forgets the exactly-three-teachers case lands on 70, which is correctly absent - no partial credit for a near miss. Hard for the section.

AM3S-24.note: Gap method: C(7,4) = 35. The hardest item here and arguably above the enhanced ACT's ceiling - the stars-and-bars argument is not ACT content, and a student without it has no route except enumeration. Keep it, but it will behave like a 43-45 item. Distractors are all binomial coefficients off the correct one (C(6,4), C(9,4), C(10,4)), which is exactly right. CROSS-ITEM: keys fall 6/6/6/6 across the four slots, a suspiciously exact balance - it is not exploitable because no group of four forms a permutation and the per-group runs are irregular, but it shows deliberate post-hoc balancing rather than an independent shuffle. The one real brief-rigidity pattern is structural, not positional: 15 of 24 option sets contain either the complement of the key or the boundary-flipped reading, and several contain both. A blind solver cannot use this - the key is the smaller member of the complementary pair in 05/08/13/22 and the larger in 10/15/21 - but it means the batch tests the same misconception family (inclusive-vs-exclusive boundary, complement not subtracted) repeatedly, and a student who learns that lesson once gets a lift on the rest.
